roles: founder of the Chabad (Lubavitch) school of Hasidism
summary: Shneur Zalman of Liady (1745-1812), known in Chabad as the Alter Rebbe ('the Old Rebbe'), was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, and the founder of the Chabad (Lubavitch) school of Hasidism, which distinctively made the intellect the path to devekut: the name Chabad is an acronym of Chochmah, Binah, and Da'at (wisdom, understanding, and knowledge), the three intellectual sefirot through which, on his account, the mind is to arouse and govern the emotions in the service of God. He systematized Hasidic thought in the Tanya (Likutei Amarim, first printed 1796), the foundational text of Chabad, and codified Jewish law in the Shulchan Aruch ha-Rav. He was imprisoned by the Russian authorities in 1798 on a denunciation and released, an event Chabad commemorates.
description:
Shneur Zalman, born in Liozna in 1745 and later settled at Liady (Lyady) in the Russian Empire, is known in the Chabad-Lubavitch movement he founded as the Alter Rebbe, 'the Old Rebbe', and among halakhists as ha-Rav, 'the Rav', after his code of law. In the movement's account he was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, the principal successor of the Baal Shem Tov, at whose court in Volhynia Shneur Zalman studied and from which he, like the other disciples of the Maggid's circle, went out to establish a Hasidic centre of his own, his in the region of White Russia (Belarus). He died in 1812 while fleeing the advance of Napoleon's army into Russia.

The school Shneur Zalman founded, Chabad, takes its name from an acronym of the three uppermost, intellectual sefirot: Chochmah (wisdom), Binah (understanding), and Da'at (knowledge). This naming carries the school's distinctive emphasis, given here as his and the movement's attributed teaching rather than as claims the editor affirms. Where the contemplative Hasidism of the Maggid's circle and the affective piety traced to the Besht are often characterized as turning on the emotions and on self-annihilation before the divine, Chabad as Shneur Zalman shaped it makes the intellect the disciplined path to devekut (cleaving to God): the mind, through sustained contemplation (hitbonenut) of the divine, is to generate and rule the emotions (the middot), so that love and awe of God arise from understanding rather than displacing it. In the Tanya he teaches that every Jew possesses two souls, an animal soul and a 'divine soul' which is 'truly a part of God above', and that the ten faculties of the soul, divided into the three intellectual powers (chochmah, binah, da'at) and the seven emotional attributes, correspond to the supernal sefirot; the beinoni, the 'intermediate' person who is neither wholly righteous nor wicked but who masters thought, speech, and deed, is set as the attainable ideal. Scholars of the school, chief among them Naftali Loewenthal, describe this as a project of 'communicating the infinite', the rendering of an esoteric mystical theology into a teaching that a broad community could study and internalize.

Shneur Zalman is distinctive among the early Hasidic masters in that he committed his teaching to writing in systematic form. His central work is the Tanya, so called from its opening word, also titled Likutei Amarim ('a collection of sayings') and Sefer shel Beinonim ('the Book of the Intermediates'), first printed in 1796; it became the foundational text of Chabad and is studied within the movement as its authoritative statement of doctrine. In its second chapter he grounds the intellectualist system explicitly in the Kabbalah of Safed, invoking Moses Cordovero's Pardes Rimonim and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal' (Isaac Luria), the 'contractions' of the light of Ein Sof through the vessels of Chabad in the world of Atzilut, so that his teaching presents itself as a continuation of Lurianic theosophy turned toward the inner life of the mind. Alongside the Tanya he composed a recension of the code of Jewish law, the Shulchan Aruch ha-Rav (the 'Rav's Shulchan Aruch'), reworking Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch with its reasons and later authorities; he was thus at once a Hasidic master and a halakhist of standing, and both identities are recorded here factually.

In 1798 Shneur Zalman was arrested and imprisoned by the Russian authorities in St Petersburg on a denunciation, connected in the accounts to the conflict between the Hasidim and their opponents the Mitnagdim and to suspicions of the young movement, and was released; the movement dates a festival (the nineteenth of Kislev) to his release and treats it as a foundational event in its history. His descendants continued the leadership of Chabad as a dynasty, which took its name from the town of Lubavitch where the line later resided. This entry presents Shneur Zalman on the tradition's own terms as the founder of Chabad and the author of the Tanya, with the intellectualist reading of Hasidism attributed to him and to his school, and with the scholarship recorded alongside.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Shneur Zalman of Liady, the Alter Rebbe, on Judaism's own terms as a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, the founder of the Chabad (Lubavitch) school, and the author of the Tanya. Chabad's DISTINCTIVE intellectualism, the intellect (Chochmah-Binah-Da'at) as the disciplined path to devekut, whereby the mind generates and governs the emotions, is stated throughout as his and the movement's ATTRIBUTED teaching ('given here as his and the movement's attributed teaching', 'on his account'), described and NOT affirmed or denied by the editor (neutrality #1, #4). His dual identity as Hasidic master and halakhist (the Shulchan Aruch ha-Rav, reworking Joseph Karo's code) is stated factually. The 1798 imprisonment and release, and the movement's commemoration of the release (19 Kislev), are reported as the movement's account and as historical event, not adjudicated. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (a) academic historians of the school, Naftali Loewenthal, Communicating the Infinite: The Emergence of the Habad School (Chicago, 1990), and Roman A. Foxbrunner, Habad: The Hasidism of R. Shneur Zalman of Lyady (Alabama, 1992); (b) the tradition's own primary text, open and auditable on Sefaria, the Tanya (Likutei Amarim), read line-by-line; and (c) Shneur Zalman himself as a contemporary-of-his-tradition primary voice, plus the modern Jewish scholarship named above. No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no YIVO Encyclopedia, no Chabad.org, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. lifespan.note: 1745-1812 CE. Born in Liozna (in present-day Belarus, then the Russian Empire); settled at Liady (Lyady), whence his epithet; a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch (d. 1772). Imprisoned by the Russian authorities in St Petersburg in 1798 on a denunciation and released (the release commemorated by Chabad on 19 Kislev). He died in 1812 during the flight from Napoleon's invasion of Russia.
